evidence.s1_requirements: Every requirement in steps/1.md is met. `snapshot()`/`restore()` are on BehaviourTree (step1.patch 1599-1613). `BehaviourTreeSnapshot` and `NodeSnapshot` are exported from src/index.ts (1751). The snapshot is plain data: getSnapshot builds new literal objects, and the action promise value is turned into a string (Action.ts:201-209). It holds node state, children, repeat/retry target and current counts (Repeat/Retry getSnapshot), the lotto selectedChild index (Lotto), the wait totalDuration and waitedDuration (Wait.ts:111-119). A restored wait starts again from now minus the time already waited (Wait.ts:132), which covers both time modes. A finished tree restores as finished, and the next step() resets it through the existing BehaviourTree.step (BehaviourTree.ts:100). The README has a section with an example (step1.patch 9-60).
evidence.s1_correctness: Each class with private runtime state overrides getSnapshot/applySnapshot: Node `_state`; Composite and Decorator children; Lotto selectedChild; Repeat and Retry counts; Wait durations; Action promise flags. A grep of the private fields in src/nodes shows nothing left out. Guards and GuardPath hold no runtime state. In Date mode the snapshot computes the waited time live (Wait.ts:113-116), so time since the last step counts and time between snapshot and restore does not. Action adds `updatePromiseId` (Action.ts:120-137, 223) so a promise left over from before a restore is ignored. A lotto resolved by a guard before picking (selectedChild null and not RUNNING) is accepted. Tests compare the original and restored trees step by step, at every snapshot point, for sequence, selector, parallel, race, all, flip/succeed/fail, fixed and random repeat/retry, lotto, fixed and random wait, branches, guards with callbacks, and the guard-resolved lotto (spec 97-236). Both wait time modes have tests with sinon fake timers (299-351), as do finished trees (252-286) and negative delta time.
evidence.s2_validation: The definition id is a cyrb53 hash of a canonical JSON form: root definitions sorted by id, keys sorted, and `args`/`succeedOnAbort` defaults filled in (step2.patch 459-503). It is checked before node validation and fails with the message "the snapshot does not match the tree's definition" (525-528). Arrays no longer pass isObject (450-451). Validation runs fully before applySnapshot, so a rejected restore changes nothing; tests compare snapshot and details before and after, including on a tree with a pending action (spec 652-680). MDSL↔JSON equivalence is tested both ways on a definition with guards, an entry callback, branch, lotto weights and a random wait (610-624). Invalid inputs (null, undefined, string, number, [], [valid], {}, objects missing fields) are rejected (626-650). A pending action is saved as READY (Action.ts:197-199), and the README documents this as a 'Limitation' paragraph (step2.patch 14). Weak point: the canonical form only knows the two defaults the MDSL parser fills in today. A JSON definition with any other extra or default-valued property would be rejected as a different definition. Registered subtrees are left out of the id (this is documented).
evidence.s3_fixes: step3.patch only adds tests (commit 0f14252); no source changed. From the code, neither report reproduces in the step-2 state. applySnapshot writes `_state` directly instead of calling setState (Node.ts:338-340), so onNodeStateChange is never called. getSnapshot builds fresh objects and applySnapshot copies promiseResult (Action.ts:220), so nothing is shared with the tree. The regression tests cover both reports at nine snapshot points: no callbacks during restore, and the next step reports the same changes as the original tree (spec 464-483). The snapshot does not change while either tree is stepped, and a snapshot taken right after restore equals it (485-503); a settled promise result case is added too. Gap: the tests only use getDeltaTime. In Date mode a snapshot taken after restore includes the milliseconds that passed (Wait.ts:115, 132), so 'equal to s' only holds within the same millisecond, and that case has no test.
evidence.design: Each node type owns its state through overrides of getSnapshot/applySnapshot, following the existing getDetails pattern in Node/Composite/Decorator. The public API is two typed methods plus exported types. Snapshot code sits in its own BehaviourTreeSnapshot.ts, next to BehaviourTreeDefinitionValidator. Weak points: NodeSnapshot is one flat type with optional fields for every node type instead of a discriminated union. Each type's validation lives in a central `switch (details.type)` in BehaviourTreeSnapshot.ts rather than in the node classes, and needs non-null assertions (`snapshot.targetCount!`). The hand-written hash and canonicalise replacer add code that depends on how the MDSL parser fills defaults.
evidence.tests: A new test/BehaviourTreeSnapshot.spec.ts uses mocha, chai and sinon like the existing tests. Its harness passes every snapshot through JSON, checks that restore calls no agent function and draws no random numbers, then steps both trees together comparing getTreeNodeDetails and agent call logs at every step. This is a strong check of 'behaves exactly as'. Also covered: both wait time modes, finished trees with new random draws, invalid-data cases, definition mismatch cases (args, wait duration, weights, guard args, structure), MDSL/JSON equivalence, pending, settled and rejected promises, stale promises, and the step-3 regressions. No existing test was changed or removed.
evidence.docs: The README has snapshot()/restore(snapshot) sections that list what a snapshot keeps and what restore guarantees, with a correct MDSL example (step1.patch 9-60). The pending-promise limitation sits next to the API (step2.patch 14), and the definition id and the excluded registered subtrees are explained. There is a Version History row for 4.4.0. package.json and package-lock.json go to 4.4.0, a minor bump for a new feature, which matches the table. Step 2 rightly did not bump the version again, since the feature was still unreleased. dist was rebuilt as the repository does.
evidence.process: The 12 commits are focused, with conventional messages (spec, feat, docs, chore version bump, review fixes, build dist, test). Step 2 splits the definition check and the pending-action change into separate feat commits. Step 3 has a single test commit, which fits since no source fix was needed. No dependencies were added. Small extras: a `version` field, the exported `NodeSnapshot`, and rewinding the same tree. They are reasonable and stay within the feature.

unmet_requirements: Step 3 report 2 (partly): in the default Date time mode, a snapshot taken after restore(s) differs from s by the milliseconds that passed (Wait.ts:115,132), and no test covers this case.
strengths: Each node type saves and restores its own state, including random counts, the lotto pick, and both wait time modes; an updatePromiseId guards against stale promises.

Very thorough tests: the original and restored trees are stepped side by side from every snapshot point for every node type, plus invalid-input, definition-mismatch, MDSL/JSON-equivalence and promise cases.
Validation runs fully before anything is applied, so a rejected restore leaves the tree untouched; the README, limitation note, Version History and version bump follow the repository's conventions.
issues: Definition matching relies on a canonical form that only fills the two defaults (`args`, `succeedOnAbort`) the MDSL parser sets today; an equivalent JSON definition with any other extra or default-valued property would be rejected.

In step 3 the code was correctly left unchanged, but report 2's 'snapshot right after restore equals s' only holds in getDeltaTime mode; in Date mode the waited time keeps growing, and no test covers it.
NodeSnapshot is a flat type with optional fields for every node type, and per-type validation sits in a central switch with non-null assertions instead of in the node classes.
review.verdict: This is a careful, well-tested snapshot/restore feature: each node type keeps its own state, validation is strict and runs before anything changes, and the docs follow the repository's conventions. Only small weak points remain (definition hashing that depends on parser defaults, and snapshot equality in Date mode), so I would merge it after minor follow-ups.
